rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Medical Image Analysis (2026) 107 Article Number: 103787. Date of Publication: 1 Jan 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) is responsible for half of all glaucoma-related blindness worldwide. The devastating disease is often clinically silent before causing irreversible visual damage. Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is the major diagnostic criterion for glaucoma. Patients with severe PACG have been clinically found to have significantly lower pupillary reflex velocity and higher iris rigidity. Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) enables dynamic visualization of the ocular iris anatomy which cannot otherwise be acquired by other imaging modalities. However, automatic quantification of dynamic iris motion on AS-OCT has not yet been implemented. The main challenges lie in the frequent jitter of high-resolution optical imaging, irregular temporal variations of elastic features, and relatively scarce datasets. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised constraint-based jitter refinement tracking (CJRTrack) framework for long-term AS-OCT video tracking. CJRTrack primarily consists of three modules: it first extracts a set of key regions from low-resolution images using an off-the-shelf point tracking algorithm. Given the initialized frames and points, an unsupervised multi-frame differentiable registration network estimates the localized deformation field patch for corresponding high-resolution images. It then refines these predictions using a temporal topology constraint-based module, which explicitly ensures overall trajectory stabilization and tracking. Multi-scale evaluations on two independent AS-OCT datasets demonstrate that CJRTrack significantly outperforms existing tracking models in both accuracy and stability. The clinical adaptivity of the model is further assessed on a glaucoma dataset containing 543 diseased eyes. Jitter-corrected quantification is extracted and used to classify neuropathic damage in primary angle closure patients.

rows.TITLE: TITLE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Can a Natural Image-Based Foundation Model Outperform a Retina-Specific Model in Detecting Ocular and Systemic Diseases?

rows.TITLE: SOURCE
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Ophthalmology Science (2026) 6:1 Article Number: 100923. Date of Publication: 1 Jan 2026

rows.TITLE: ABSTRACT
rows.D(2)PF-net: A dual-decoder progressive f: Purpose: DINOv2 is a natural image-based foundation model (FM), pretrained exclusively on 142 million natural images from the LVD-142M data set. In contrast, RETFound is a retina-specific FM, pretrained on ∼3 million images, including natural images, color fundus photos, and OCT images (∼1 million each). Despite DINOv2's massive pretraining data set, its application in ophthalmology and relative performance to domain-specific FMs remain understudied. To address this gap, we conducted a head-to-head comparative evaluation between DINOv2 and RETFound models across a range of downstream ocular and systemic disease tasks. Design: Retrospective head-to-head evaluation. Subjects: Ocular disease detection tasks included diabetic retinopathy (DR), glaucoma, and multiclass eye diseases, whereas systemic disease incidence prediction focused on the 3-year incidence of heart failure, myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke. Eight open-source data sets (APTOS-2019, IDRID, MESSIDOR2 for DR; PAPILA, Glaucoma Fundus for glaucoma; JSIEC, Retina, OCTID for multiclass eye diseases) and the Moorfields AlzEye data set (for systemic diseases) were used for fine-tuning and internal testing. External test sets included the same open-source data sets (cross-dataset validation) and the UK Biobank (for systemic diseases). Methods: We replicated the fine-tuning methodology from the original RETFound study on 3 DINOv2 models (large, base, small). All models were fine-tuned on the respective data sets and evaluated through internal and external testing. Main Outcome Measures: Area under the receiver operating characteristics curve and 2-sided t-tests were used to compare models' performances. Results: For ocular disease detection, DINOv2 models generally outperformed RETFound. For DR, DINOv2-Large achieved AUCs of 0.850 to 0.952, exceeding RETFound's 0.823 to 0.944 (all P ≤ 0.007). For multiclass eye diseases, DINOv2-large (AUC = 0.892, Retina data set) surpassed RETFound (AUC = 0.846, P < 0.001). For glaucoma, DINOv2-base (AUC = 0.958, Glaucoma Fundus) outperformed RETFound (AUC = 0.940, P < 0.001). Conversely, for systemic disease incidence prediction, RETFound achieved superior AUCs of 0.796 (heart failure), 0.732 (myocardial infarction), and 0.754 (ischemic stroke), outperforming DINOv2's best models' AUC (0.663–0.771, all P < 0.001). This trend persisted in external validation. Conclusions: Our findings reveal the merits of DINOv2 in ocular disease detection tasks, whereas RETFound demonstrates an edge in systemic disease incidence prediction. These findings showcase the distinct scenarios where general-purpose and domain-specific FMs excel, highlighting the importance of aligning FM selection with task-specific requirements to optimize clinical performance. Financial Disclosure(s): Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

manuscript.abstract_md:
# Abstract

**Background.** Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) systems
have been developed for glaucoma detection on color fundus photographs and
structural optical coherence tomography (OCT) images, and growing evidence
suggests they may match or exceed human-reader performance. To our knowledge,
no prior systematic review has combined AI and human-reader arms in a unified
Bayesian diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) framework that permits probabilistic
superiority statements.

**Methods.** We conducted a PRISMA-DTA–conformant systematic review and an
arm-based Bayesian hierarchical bivariate diagnostic network meta-analysis
(NMA) of studies reporting per-patient, per-eye, or per-image sensitivity
and specificity of AI-only, human-reader, or hybrid AI + human decision arms
for glaucoma detection. We searched PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase, Cochrane
CENTRAL, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science from database inception to
April 30, 2026 (frozen April 14, 2026). Two reviewers independently
screened titles, abstracts, and full texts; disagreements were resolved
by consensus. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-3 (2024 AI extension).
Certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE for diagnostic tests. The
Bayesian hierarchical bivariate DTA model was fitted in JAGS via R2jags
(four chains, 20,000 iterations per chain, 10,000 burn-in). Subgroup
analyses stratified the network by glaucoma target (any glaucoma, GON,
referable, POAG, suspect) and by imaging modality. Sensitivity analyses
restricted the dataset to confirmed glaucoma, external validation only,
no vendor involvement, and prospective designs. Heterogeneity was
quantified by between-study τ on the logit scale and I². Publication
bias was assessed by Deeks' regression. The protocol was registered with
INPLASY (INPLASY202610001).

**Results.** From 52,286 records identified, 3,664 remained after
cross-source dedup and 697 advanced to full-text screening. We included
145 studies for the systematic review and 144 studies (217 arm-level rows;
189 AI-only, 28 reader-only, 3 hybrid AI + human) for the quantitative
meta-analysis. Pooled AI-only sensitivity was 0.925 (95 % credible
interval [CrI] 0.913–0.936) and specificity 0.940 (0.932–0.948). Pooled
reader-only sensitivity was 0.846 (0.795–0.889) and specificity 0.892
(0.853–0.924). The posterior difference favoured AI on both dimensions:
ΔSensitivity +0.079 (0.037–0.128; Pr[AI > Reader] = 100 %) and
ΔSpecificity +0.049 (0.018–0.087; Pr = 99.97 %). On the joint SUCRA
ranking, the AI node scored 100 % and the reader node 0 %. Between-study
heterogeneity was substantial (τ_sens ≈ 0.5, τ_spec ≈ 0.5 logit-scale;
I² > 90 %). Meta-regression identified glaucoma target, imaging modality,
and vendor involvement as significant moderators. Risk of bias on the
patient-selection domain was rated High in 78.6 % of contributing studies.
The certainty of evidence was MODERATE for the AI node and LOW for the
reader node.

**Conclusions.** In this arm-based Bayesian DTA NMA of 144 studies, AI
systems applied to colour fundus and structural OCT images achieved higher
pooled sensitivity and specificity than human readers for glaucoma
detection, with near-certain posterior superiority on both dimensions.
The MODERATE-to-LOW certainty of evidence reflects substantial residual
heterogeneity and risk of bias in patient-selection across the included
literature; the headline numbers should be interpreted as the upper bound
of plausibly attainable performance under current case-mix.

**Registration.** INPLASY202610001.

# Results

## Study selection and characteristics

From 52,286 records identified through the five-database search,
3,664 remained after cross-source de-duplication. After title/abstract
screening, 697 records advanced to full-text assessment; 158 PDFs were
retrieved into the `04_fulltext/` archive. Following the eligibility
criteria locked on 2026-04-14, **145 studies** were judged eligible
for the systematic review and **144 studies** had extractable 2 × 2
confusion data for the quantitative meta-analysis. These 144 studies
contributed **217 arm-level analytic rows**: 189 AI-only arms across
150 unique AI cohorts, 28 reader-only arms across 16 studies that
included a separately reported human-reader benchmark, and 3 hybrid
AI + human arms (Figure 1, PRISMA-DTA flow).

The included studies were published between 2016 and 2026 (122/144
in 2020 or later), spanning North America, Europe, Asia, and Oceania.
Imaging modality was split between colour fundus photography (n ≈ 95
studies) and structural OCT (n ≈ 49 studies); a small number of
studies reported both modalities. Glaucoma target distribution in the
12_Analysis_Ready set was: glaucoma 124, GON 21, referable glaucoma 12,
glaucoma suspect 5, POAG 5. Reference standards comprised expert
clinical adjudication, visual-field criteria, structural OCT criteria,
and combined criteria. Vendor involvement (vendor-author or vendor-funded)
was disclosed in a minority of studies and was carried forward as a
meta-regression covariate.

## Pooled diagnostic performance

The arm-based Bayesian hierarchical bivariate DTA NMA produced the
following posterior summaries (Table 2, eTable 02; Figure 2 forest,
Figure 3 HSROC):

| Node | Studies | Arms | Sensitivity (95 % CrI) | Specificity (95 % CrI) |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| AI-only | 150 | 189 | 0.925 (0.913, 0.936) | 0.940 (0.932, 0.948) |
| Reader-only | 16 | 28 | 0.846 (0.795, 0.889) | 0.892 (0.853, 0.924) |

The posterior contrast favoured AI on both dimensions:

- ΔSensitivity (AI − Reader) = +0.079 (95 % CrI 0.037–0.128);
  Pr(AI > Reader) = 100 %.
- ΔSpecificity (AI − Reader) = +0.049 (95 % CrI 0.018–0.087);
  Pr(AI > Reader) = 99.97 %.

On the SUCRA joint ranking the AI node achieved 100 % and the reader
node 0 % (eTable 10, eFigure 10).

## Heterogeneity and meta-regression

Between-study heterogeneity was substantial. The posterior τ on the
logit scale was approximately 0.5 for both sensitivity and specificity;
I² exceeded 90 % at both nodes (eTable 07, Table_Heterogeneity).
Univariable meta-regression (eTable 04) identified the following
covariates as associated with diagnostic accuracy (P < 0.05):
glaucoma target (referable vs confirmed), imaging modality (OCT vs
fundus), reference standard category, and vendor involvement.
Multivariable meta-regression (eTable 05) retained glaucoma target
and vendor involvement as independent moderators after adjustment for
geography and publication year.

## Subgroup analyses

| Subgroup (target) | AI Sens (95 % CrI) | AI Spec (95 % CrI) | n studies |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Any glaucoma | 0.92 (0.91, 0.94) | 0.95 (0.94, 0.96) | 117 |
| GON | 0.93 (0.89, 0.96) | 0.95 (0.92, 0.97) | 15 |
| Referable glaucoma | 0.92 (0.85, 0.96) | 0.94 (0.91, 0.96) | 8 |
| POAG | 0.94 (0.86, 0.98) | 0.92 (0.86, 0.96) | 4 |
| Glaucoma suspect | 0.86 (0.74, 0.94) | 0.91 (0.84, 0.96) | 4 |

(Numbers above from the FAST_PROXY_RUN posterior; full-length MCMC
publication numbers will be reported in the final version.)

## Sensitivity analyses

Pre-specified sensitivity analyses (Table_Sensitivity_Analyses,
eFigure 06) restricting the dataset to:

1. complete 2 × 2 reported only,
2. confirmed or detected glaucoma only,
3. external validation only,
4. no vendor involvement, and
5. prospective enrollment only

produced posterior estimates within ±0.02 of the headline AI–Reader
contrast on both sensitivity and specificity, and the posterior
probability that AI exceeded Reader remained > 95 % in every analysis.
Leave-one-out diagnostics (eTable 11; eFigures 13–14) showed that no
single study moved the headline contrast by more than 0.01.

## Publication bias

The Deeks' funnel asymmetry test applied to the network log-DOR did
not reach formal significance, but visual asymmetry and node-stratified
asymmetry suggested possible small-study or reporting bias (eFigure 11,
eFigure 12).

## Risk of bias

QUADAS-3 ratings (eTable 01, eFigure 09 traffic-light) identified
the Patient Selection domain as the dominant concern: rated High in
78.6 % of contributing studies, driven by case-control / enrichment
designs in older datasets. Index Test was rated Low in 90.3 % and
Reference Standard in 53.8 %.

## Clinical impact

At the median observed prevalence of glaucoma in the dataset,
applying the pooled AI-only operating point to 10,000 screened
individuals would yield approximately 1,388 true positives,
113 false negatives, 7,524 true negatives, and 480 false positives
(eFigure 02, Clinical_Impact_Scenarios.csv). The corresponding
reader-only counts at the pooled operating point would be
1,269 true positives, 232 false negatives, 7,135 true negatives,
and 870 false positives — a difference of approximately
+119 detected cases per 10,000 screened in favour of AI.

## Certainty of evidence

GRADE-DTA rating (Table 4, grade_summary_findings.md) was MODERATE
for the AI node and LOW for the reader node. Downgrades were applied
for risk of bias (Patient Selection) and inconsistency
(network-level heterogeneity).
